newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Infotech trade pact seen attracting 41 countries.
newsitem.headline: Infotech trade pact seen attracting 41 countries.

text.p: A total of 41 countries could sign up next week for a $500 billion pact to remove tariffs in the booming global trade in information technology products (IT) by the year 2000, trade sources said on Friday.

They said Panama had announced it was joining the deal, shaped in December during a World Trade Organisation (WTO) ministerial meeting in Singapore, and the Czech Republic and Slovakia had promised to finalise their offers on Monday.

The pact covers five main categories of products -- computers, telecommunications products, semiconductors, semiconductor manufacturing equipment, software including diskettes and CD ROMs, and scientific instruments.
It was originally championed by the United States.

But after intensive negotiations among the top trading powers in the second half of last year, the European Union agreed to come on board in Singapore and other key developed and developing countries followed suit.
Last month, Malaysia and Thailand came in, pushing the coverage of the pact -- to go into effect on July 1 -- over the threshold agreed in Singapore of 90 per cent of world IT trade.

Trade officials said countries accounting for over 92 per cent were now lined up to start lifting customs duties from the middle of this year through equal annual reductions to be concluded on January 1, 2000.
Some developing countries have been granted a longer timeframe, but exact details are still under discussion.

The United States, the EU and Japan are known to be unhappy with proposals from key Asian states -- including Malaysia and Thailand and also India -- to maintain tariffs on some products until 2005 or 2007.

With Panama's adherence to the IT deal, confirmed participants are Australia, Canada, Costa Rica, Estonia, the 15 members of the EU, Hong Kong, Iceland, India, Indonesia, Israel, Japan, South Korea, Macau, Malaysia, New Zealand, Norway, Poland, Romania, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand, Turkey and the United States.

U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky, who has argued the deal will slash costs for consumers as well as businesses and give a kick to the global economy, said earlier this month coverage was now enough for an accord.

Although the pact was negotiated outside the WTO framework, it will be incorporated into the rules of the world trade body and signatories will be obliged to extend its terms to all other members of the organisation.

WTO Director-General Renato Ruggiero said last month the accord, together with the global agreement reached in February to liberalise trade in telecommunications, marked a major advance for rich and poor states.
The two had "the potential to unlock enormous gains in development and growth and.... benefit all countries, developed and developing alike," said Ruggiero.

"Knowledge is the most essential raw material of the global economy and with the progress we have made in these negotiations we are clearly laying the foundation for the trading system of the 21st century," he declared.
